claims.statement: Enron filed for bankruptcy in December 2001; the FBI describes the resulting case as the most complex white-collar crime investigation in its history.
In January 2002 agents searched Enron's 50-story headquarters for nine days, recovered more than 400 boxes of evidence, and conducted more than 100 interviews.
The investigation ultimately involved more than 1,800 interviews, more than 3,000 boxes of evidence, over four terabytes of collected digital data, and email from more than 600 employees.
Financial analysis supported restraining orders and the seizure of more than 168 million dollars in assets; more than 105 million dollars was forfeited to help compensate victims.
The SEC alleged that Jeffrey Skilling, Richard Causey, and others manipulated Enron's publicly reported financial results and made false or misleading statements about its condition and performance.
The SEC alleged that executives chose to beat analysts' second-quarter 2000 estimate by two cents and caused millions of dollars of reserves to be released into earnings to report 34 cents per share.

The SEC alleged that Enron moved a large losing portion of Enron Energy Services into Enron Wholesale in 2001 so Wholesale earnings and reserve accounts could absorb hundreds of millions of dollars in EES losses.

The SEC alleged that misleading claims about Enron Broadband Services helped raise Enron's stock and that Project Greyhawk enabled Enron to recognize about 85 million dollars in earnings tied to that increase.

claims.locator: Use of SPEs and LJM Partnerships — Raptor I
claims.statement: The SEC alleged that Raptor I was presented as a hedge with an independent party even though the counterparty was not independent, its investment was not genuinely at risk, and an undisclosed side agreement protected its return.

The SEC alleged that Enron temporarily moved an interest in the poorly performing Cuiaba project to LJM for 11.3 million dollars under an undisclosed repurchase understanding and improperly recognized about 65 million dollars of income.

A federal jury convicted Jeffrey Skilling in 2006 of conspiracy, twelve securities-fraud counts, insider trading, and five false-statement counts; in 2013 he was resentenced to 168 months and ordered to forfeit about 42 million dollars for victims.

claims.locator: Scheme effects on stock price and bankruptcy
claims.statement: The DOJ said the scheme made Enron appear healthy and predictable, helped its stock rise from about 30 dollars in early 1998 to above 80 dollars in January 2001, and ended with December 2001 bankruptcy and virtually worthless stock.
The five-year investigation produced jury convictions of senior officials and guilty pleas from others; the FBI reports that 22 people were convicted for actions related to the fraud.
